speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Scam losses fell slightly but are still high.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the Global Fraud Summit which I attended last month, other countries shared that they were facing similar challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have implemented multiple measures to combat scams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has been working with telecommunication companies to block all incoming calls from overseas that spoof local numbers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a result, the volume of such calls attempted has dropped.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2022, there were approximately 970 million of such attempts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2023, there were 18 million attempts, a far smaller number but all were blocked.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2023, IMDA introduced the SMS Sender ID Registry, which requires organisations to register the alphanumeric Sender IDs which they want to use in SMS communications with their customers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: SMSes using non-registered Sender IDs will be marked as “Likely-SCAM”.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a result, phishing, which was the main type of scam perpetrated through SMSes, has claimed fewer victims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Amounts lost to phishing scams have also fallen.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With these measures in place, scammers have quickly changed their tactics and pivoted to using local SIM cards to reach prospective victims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: People who receive scam calls and SMSes from locally registered numbers may think they are legitimate and fall prey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2023, over 23,000 local mobile lines were involved in scams and other cybercrimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is four times the number in 2021.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is three times the amount lost in 2021.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Local numbers have also been used by scammers to set up WhatsApp and Telegram accounts to target victims or receive their monies via PayNow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This comes on top of their being used for other crimes, such as unlicensed moneylending.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To enforce against scammers who abuse local SIM cards, the Police has worked with foreign counterparts as these scammers are mainly based overseas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In February 2023, the Singapore Police Force (SPF) worked with the Royal Malaysia Police to conduct simultaneous raids at three apartment complexes in Johor.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They arrested 12 Malaysians for their involvement in using six prepaid Singapore SIM cards to perpetrate fake friend calls.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The syndicate is believed to have been involved in more than 360 reports, with more than $1.3 million of losses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But enforcement after the fact is scant comfort for the victims.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We want to go upstream, to prevent the scam from happening in the first place, by strengthening deterrence and accountability in the use of local SIM cards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Hence, clause 3 of this Bill introduces new offences to target three groups of people who misuse local SIM cards to facilitate scams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These are people who give away their local SIM cards or provide their particulars to others to be used to sign up for local SIM cards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Often, they do so to earn a quick buck.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Based on a sampling study, close to 80% of local SIM cards misused for crime were registered with another person's particulars.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Every SIM card in the hands of a scammer is a weapon.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Armed with even just one SIM card, a scammer can do a great deal of harm.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In a 2021 case, a single local mobile line was linked to 48 job scam reports, with losses amounting to approximately $1 million.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In most of the cases, the Police have faced difficulties in taking these irresponsible subscribers to task.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Current laws put the onus on the Police to prove that the subscriber knowingly gave away their local SIM cards for unlawful purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Irresponsible subscribers can easily claim that they were unaware of the consequences of their actions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, in 2023, a subscriber signed up for 11 postpaid SIM cards and sold them to a friend and claimed that his friend said the mobile lines were needed to create accounts on cryptocurrency platforms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Six out of the 11 mobile lines were later found to have been used in scam cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When interviewed, the subscriber claimed that he did not know that the mobile lines would be used for unlawful purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As there was no evidence to suggest otherwise, the Police could not take any action against him.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill will introduce new offences in sections 37B and 37C of the Miscellaneous Offences (Public Order and Nuisance) Act, or abbreviated as MOA, targeting irresponsible subscribers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will be an offence for a person to hand over local SIM cards registered with his own particulars to another person; or allow his own particulars to be used to sign up for a local SIM card by another person.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A person will be liable, if he did so, knowing or having reasonable grounds to believe, that the local SIM card would be used for unlawful purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With these new laws, a person in these scenarios will no longer be able to simply claim ignorance as a defence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The law puts the onus on the person to prove that he was unaware.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To be clear, Sir, it is not our intent to criminalise people who give away their local SIM cards for legitimate purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, some people register SIM cards in their names for family members' use, including elderly parents and children.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is also not our intent to penalise people who were genuinely tricked into giving up their credentials, which were subsequently used to register for local SIM cards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second group we are targeting are middlemen involved in procuring or providing local SIM cards to scam syndicates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Police have caught people transferring or possessing local SIM cards not registered with their own particulars.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In most of the instances, they were doing so without legitimate reason.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Similar to irresponsible subscribers, the Police have faced difficulties in prosecuting such middlemen, as it is difficult to prove that they had intended to abet an offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In one case, the Police identified a middleman who collected fraudulently registered local SIM cards from an accomplice and then sent the SIM cards to scammers in Malaysia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the point of arrest, the middleman was found to be in possession of 290 prepaid SIM cards that were fraudulently registered.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In total, the middleman was found to have purchased over 1,000 prepaid SIM cards that were fraudulently registered, between 2010 and 2021.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Although the middleman was initially charged in Court, he was eventually given a discharge amounting to an acquittal, due to evidential difficulties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They would be liable for either: first, receiving or possessing local SIM cards, with intent to use or supply them for unlawful purposes; second, supplying local SIM cards, knowing or having reasonable grounds to believe that they would be used for unlawful purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These provisions will not only cover local SIM cards registered with other persons' particulars, but will also cover unregistered local SIM cards, as these can easily be activated by scammers using stolen credentials.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Specifically for dealing with local SIM cards registered with other persons' particulars, a person may be deemed liable in three scenarios: one, he received or supplied the local SIM card for any gain; two, he did not take reasonable steps to find out the identity and physical location of the recipient of the local SIM card; three, he did not take reasonable steps to find out the recipient's purpose for obtaining the local SIM card.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill also introduces a new section 39E in the MOA to deal with people who buy, sell or rent a local SIM card registered with another person's particulars.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As this involves an exchange of money, it is more serious than simply receiving or supplying local SIM cards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is no reason why someone other than a contracted retailer should be trading local SIM cards registered in another person's particulars, in exchange for money or other benefits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As such, the provision is drafted such that the Prosecution would not need to prove criminal intent in making out an offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is not our intent to catch those who receive, supply or possess local SIM cards for lawful purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For instance, employers holding on to SIM cards intended for their employees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, if they make an explanation, then this would be taken into consideration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The third group of people we are targeting is errant retailers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: IMDA requires mobile service providers to implement measures to prevent fraudulent registrations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The mobile service providers may appoint third-party retailers to sell SIM cards and perform registrations, and subject these retailers to similar requirements by way of contractual obligations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, retailers are required to verify the identity of subscribers by visually checking the subscribers against their original IDs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are also required to scan subscribers' IDs instead of manually keying in the subscribers' personal particulars.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mobile service providers may be in breach of the regulatory obligations, if they or their appointed retailers had lapses in implementing these requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The vast majority of retailers adhere to IMDA’s requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, a number have used stolen or false credentials to register local SIM cards, which they then sell to scammers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In a recent case, the Police arrested four handphone retailers who had used the particulars of unsuspecting subscribers to register post-paid SIM cards and then sold these SIM cards to customers, likely scammers, who wanted to conceal their identity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Not only do they tarnish the reputation of their peers, their actions cause many victims to suffer losses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, there is no offence that specifically deals with these retailers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under today’s regime, these retailers might simply lose their contracts with the mobile service provider.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Stronger deterrence is needed if we are to prevent such retailers from helping scammers easily acquire fraudulently registered SIM cards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The new section makes it a criminal offence to facilitate fraudulent registrations knowing or having reasonable grounds to believe that the local SIM card would be used for unlawful purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Errant retailers may also be liable if the local SIM card is proven to have subsequently been used for unlawful purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The new criminal offence will complement our current regulatory levers and allow heavier punishments to be imposed on errant retailers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This includes imprisonment sentences for the employees who were involved in the fraudulent registrations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The vast majority of law-abiding retailers need not be concerned.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The penalties for the new SIM card offences will be pegged to those for the misuse of Singpass credentials under the Computer Misuse Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: All the new offences will also apply to corporations and unincorporated associations, such as partnerships and societies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, as such entities cannot be subject to imprisonment, the maximum fines for these entities will be twice the amount for individuals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 4 of the Bill introduces standard provisions for the attribution of liability for MOA offences committed by entities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is necessary, as most scam syndicates operate from overseas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The new section 39I will provide for all local SIM card offences to be arrestable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Next, the Bill amends the MOA to allow the transmission of false messages for certain legitimate purposes, such as to facilitate the conduct of simulated phishing exercises to enhance awareness and vigilance against scams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, section 14D of the MOA – which can be traced back to the Telecommunications Act 1965 – criminalises the transmission of a message which the person knows is false or fabricated.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Because of how the provision was drafted, any transmission of a false or fabricated message could be caught, even if the transmission was for legitimate purposes, like the prevention of crime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The most pertinent example today would be simulated phishing exercises.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is done to sensitise the staff to phishing attacks, thereby reducing the risk that they and consequently the organisation, fall victim to scams, cybercrimes and malicious cyber activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With the current provision, however, the conduct of such exercises could be considered an offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill amends section 14D to introduce a defence for the transmission of false messages for legitimate purposes related to public order, public safety or national security; or the prevention, investigation or prosecution of offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This would give organisations assurance that they would not be committing an offence if they transmit false messages for legitimate purposes, such as simulated phishing exercises.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first group of the amendments will clarify powers of apprehension, under the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Act (MHCTA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mental health and well-being is a key priority in our national agenda and the Government is fully committed to doing more to improve mental health and well-being.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: During the Motion on Advancing Mental Health in February this year, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong highlighted several key moves the Government will be making, including increasing the number of public sector psychiatrists and psychologists, introducing mental health services to all polyclinics and more general practitioner (GP) clinics, and training frontline personnel and volunteers to help people struggling with mental health.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The importance of treating people with mental health conditions with respect and empathy is also not lost on our ground officers, many of whom would be familiar with their own friends or family, who may likewise struggle with mental health.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This has always been the case since the existing provisions in the MHCTA were enacted in 2008, we have also seen largely effective outcomes when Police interventions were requested.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To be clear, the current amendments do not directly relate to how such cases are treated in our medical system nor does it relate to the wider community acceptance for people with mental health conditions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The amendments we are dealing with today relate strictly to how Police can be most helpful when they are called to assist in cases when a person may harm themselves or others around them; and Police have reason to believe that the better cause of action is apprehension rather than arrest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Police are often called to respond to incidents involving persons who may pose a danger to themselves or to others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This may include cases of criminal intimidation where threats of harm are made or cases of violent behaviour in a public place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The duty of the police officers is to prevent the danger from materialising.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where criminal offences are made out, Police may make an arrest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, where such danger is reasonably suspected to be attributable to a mental disorder and it might be more appropriate to bring such persons to a medical practitioner than to a police lock-up, the Police can apprehend them under section 7 of MHCTA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is already provided for by law since 2008.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: After apprehension, as opposed to arrest, the Police will bring the person to a medical practitioner and not to a lock-up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To be clear, powers of apprehension under section 7 cannot be applied just because a person is suffering from mental health conditions, if the person does not pose a danger to themselves or others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The person must pose a danger to themselves or others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, it is completely mistaken to think of the existing section 7 as a measure to address mental health conditions when, in fact, it deals simply with situations of danger.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In other words, the Police do not get involved in cases of persons with mental health conditions unless they pose a danger to themselves or someone else.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Police will not do so and, in fact, cannot do so even with the amendments to the MHCTA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such persons will be treated and managed directly by medical practitioners.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, such persons may pose a danger to themselves, for example, threatening to commit suicide; or to others, for example, conducting themselves in a manner which may hurt their family or members of the public nearby.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In these circumstances, the public would expect and indeed want the Police to intervene, before anyone gets hurt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In a real case, a 73-year-old man was found to be in possession of an ice pick and knife at a Police station.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When asked why he had those items, he said foreign law enforcement agencies were disturbing his sleep and he would use the ice pick and knife in a bid to tell them to leave him alone.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Because of the High Court's determination, for cases where the time frame of the danger presented is unspecified or is not imminent, the Police do not have the option of apprehending the person and bringing him for medical treatment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Police officers confronted with these situations are left with two options, either not take any action and risk people getting hurt or even killed or make an arrest under criminal laws and put the person through the criminal process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first option is not responsible – the public expects Police to keep Singaporeans safe.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second option is not ideal – criminal arrest is not what the person who may have mental health conditions needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The same High Court judgment determined that apprehensions are distinct from arrests under the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This means that Police officers do not have certain powers associated with arrest, which are essential when making apprehensions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In particular, the High Court determined that the Police do not have powers of search and seizure to ensure that the person is not hiding dangerous weapons or items.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Police would be expected to hand over the person to the staff of the medical facility only after ensuring that he is not in possession of weapons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This does not mean that the person will be needlessly roughed up.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the contrary, having assessed that the person may be suffering from mental health conditions, Police offices are minded to carry out search and seizure with due care and respect.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Section 7 of the MHCTA is not meant to place additional burdens on such persons or their families.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Instead, our goals are to prevent danger from materialising and enable persons with mental health issues to access medical care in a timely manner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will now move on to the next group of amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members know that the demands on the Home Team are growing, including the Police.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some have spoken about this at the recent Committee of Supply debate and I thank them for their support and appreciation of the hard work Home Team officers do for the safety and security of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The following amendment relates to Police's obligations when non-arrestable offences are reported.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Similar provisions are already present for arrestable offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, where Police receive a report of a traffic accident with no injuries, they are empowered to not take further action, even though arrestable offences, such as dangerous or careless driving may be disclosed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, the same exceptions are currently not available for non-arrestable offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, when a non-arrestable offence is reported, the Police must either investigate the case, refer the informant to a magistrate, or refer the case to a mediator of a Community Mediation Centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This legal obligation applies even if the Police have reason to believe that the case is not of a serious nature, or there are insufficient grounds for proceeding with the matter.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This obligation results in poor use of public resources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This amendment therefore seeks to align the Police's obligations whether for offences that are arrestable or non-arrestable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will provide Police more operational flexibility to decide whether a Police report is deserving of action.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Another group of amendments enhances the Home Team's operations and reduces operational risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, these persons have to be brought to a Police officer to be released on bail or personal bond.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The amendments improve efficiency, as these arrested persons would no longer need to be brought to a Police lock-up or to a Police officer for granting of bail or personal bond.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This reduces operational risks in the transport of these arrested persons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will now speak on the third and last set of amendments, which seeks to enhance and safeguard YRSG's operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 15 of the Bill includes two amendments to the Singapore Corporation of Rehabilitative Enterprises Act, or the SCORE Act for short.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first amendment is to provide YRSG with greater flexibility on staff administration and disciplinary matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, YRSG's internal disciplinary framework is stipulated in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This means YRSG needs to enact changes in the subsidiary legislation in order to change its internal disciplinary framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is unnecessary and inconsistent with the practices of most Statutory Boards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill amends the SCORE Act to remove the need for subsidiary legislation to be made regarding administrative staff matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Consequently, the two existing pieces of subsidiary legislation on staff disciplinary matters will be revoked.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second amendment is to safeguard Yellow Ribbon symbols and representations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They include YRSG's corporate logo and symbols of initiatives related to YRSG's mission, such as the Yellow Ribbon Project and Yellow Ribbon Fund logos.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These logos are registered trademarks belonging to YRSG.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are used in YRSG's campaigns and programmes to galvanise society to support the reintegration of ex-offenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, there have been instances where these symbols were misused for ill intent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, we had received feedback from members of the public that they were approached at hawker centres by individuals selling merchandise, or individuals going door-to-door asking for donations and were shown documents with the Yellow Ribbon logo.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In these instances, the symbols were used for the individual's own benefit, under the guise of supporting ex-offenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is consistent with existing provisions governing the use of the symbols of other Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) Statutory Boards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The new SIM card offences will help disrupt the operations of criminal syndicates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Bill will also allow us to better protect the public, as well as enable our Home Team officers to carry out their duties more effectively and efficiently.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It addresses two critical areas: combating scams and enhancing Home Team operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Scams have surged globally with technological advancements and Singapore is no exception.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is despite having measures, such as SMS Sender ID Registry and blocking overseas scam calls, amongst other measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For Group A, can the Ministry clarify why 10 SIM cards is used as a threshold?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For Group C, authorisation is an essential condition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry simplify and standardise the authorisation processes for companies to implement this effectively?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because the potential losses caused to victims are high, we should consider minimum fines and jail terms for individual offenders and fines tied to a percentage of annual revenue for retailers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Effective strategies are crucial to detect and prosecute such sales of SIM cards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of them operate on platforms like Telegram or Carousell.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How would the Ministry work with the platform owners to stem out such activities?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, on the enhancements to support our Home Team operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The proposed amendments empower law enforcement agencies, particularly the Police Force, in handling mental health-related incidents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It seeks to set clear thresholds for apprehension, ensuring effectiveness and clarity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mental health experts, rightfully, are concerned that the changes could lead to wrongful apprehensions and deepen stigma of mental health patients.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, Police can only apprehend mentally disordered individuals if they pose "imminent" danger.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the measures put in place to minimise hasty assessment by untrained officers that increase the chances wrongful apprehension?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, can the Ministry also clarify what are the scenarios constituting what is "reasonably" in determining when a Police officer may make such arrest or apprehension.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I propose that the Ministry also partner the mental health community to train and prepare our officers for this new change in the law.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, we must appreciate the difficulties in making the right operational decisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is not uncommon for Police officers to encounter situations on the ground where the threat of violence can escalate very quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are many variables that can cause such escalation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They can also happen when Police officers are called down to a scene.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There can be very little time from the escalation to harm actually being caused.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our officers must be trusted and empowered to protect not only the subject but also innocent bystanders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They must also have the weight of the law behind them to discharge their duties and not have to second-guess themselves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, second-guessing in such situations can be highly dangerous.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the years that I served in the Singapore Police Force, I have witnessed a few of such situations that warrant decisive actions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our officers' deep training allows them to execute their roles decisively even while they put themselves harm's way.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These very actions make the difference between minimising harm and allowing a situation to go very wrong.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, we must provide our officers with every available tool to protect life and property.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, I support the enhancements in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, I note that it is crucial to ensure sensitive and safe apprehension procedures that are updated regularly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Partnership with the mental healthcare sector to develop standardised procedures and providing additional training and resources for law enforcement officers is essential.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, regarding apprehension in attempted suicide cases, individuals are obligated to aid Police officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry clarify that refusal to aid the officer, while regrettable is not an offence?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The amendments targeting scams offer promising solutions which can reduce the number of scam-related incidents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Additionally, sensitive treatment and effective handling of mentally disordered individuals by law enforcement agencies with clear parameters informed and supported by the mental health community will be paramount.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This amendment supersedes the interpretation of danger by the General Division of the High Court in Mah Kiat Seng vs Attorney-General and Others.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In that case, the Court held at paragraph 48 that the use of the word "danger" implied a degree of imminence, that is, that without the Police officer's intervention, such behaviour is likely to occur within a short time, which the Judge stated that he would consider to be a matter of hours rather than days.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In addition, the Court clarified that there must be a reasonably imminent risk of physical harm to the person apprehended or others.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I appreciate that the Minister for Home Affairs had previously stated in this House that law should not inadvertently result in defensive policing, I believe that it is important to make it clear that the amendments reducing the threshold to apprehend a person is subject to safeguards and for the public to know and understand what those safeguards are.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As our law currently stands, the Police's general power of arrest is subject to various safeguards under the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The distinction between arrestable and non-arrestable offences make clear the situations where a police officer may arrest someone without a warrant.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, while the police may arrest without a warrant someone on suspicion that they have caused or may voluntarily cause grievous hurt to another person, the police cannot arrest without a warrant in a situation where the offence is that of voluntarily causing hurt.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With the proposed amendments, I would like to seek clarification from the Minister of my understanding that these changes are in response to the High Court's ruling in Mah.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally and specifically, can the Minister detail what specific challenges our law enforcement officers have had while carrying out their policing duties with suspects who are persons suffering from mental health crises or illnesses that warrant these amendments?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have concerns that the threshold being lowered has to be very carefully weighed up against the expressed aims of Singaporean society to do more to properly support and address mental health challenges facing some of our fellow Singaporeans, especially when law enforcement officers do not necessarily have the training and resources to fully understand the challenging and complex issues surrounding mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have five main points and clarifications about the new threshold.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, I have a concern that the lowering of the threshold from the Court's clarification of a reasonably imminent risk being lowered to a reasonable likelihood that danger to life or personal safety may occur under the MHCTA would lead to different standards applying to those who may be living with mental health conditions or illness.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In fact, according to the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD Committee), such a distinction is discriminatory.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In September 2015, in Guidelines on the Right to Liberty and Security of Persons with Disabilities issued by the CRPD Committee, legislations like the MHCTA, which allow the detention of persons on the ground of their actual or perceived impairment on the basis that they are deemed dangerous to themselves or to others, are discriminatory in nature and amount to arbitrary deprivation of liberty.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Can the Minister clarify if the Government has considered its obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which the Government ratified in 2013, in tabling this amendment?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If so, how do the proposed amendments square with our CRPD commitments?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In October 2022, the CRPD Committee issued its concluding observations for its first periodic review of Singapore's record on disability rights.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As noted above, this refers specifically to the MHCTA.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I note that the Minister for Health had stated in a response to a Parliamentary Question (PQ) in 2021 that the MHCTA is already in compliance with the requirements of Article 14 of the CRPD.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If not, will the Government consider the necessary steps to be taken to ensure that the MHCTA complies with our obligations under the CRPD?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, the High Court Judge in Mah also noted that he considered that a time frame for imminence under the new old threshold would be a matter of hours rather than days.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Third, paragraph 23 of MHA's press release on this Bill gives an example of a situation where police records show that the person making the threat has a history of mental disorder.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would the Minister be able to confirm that all persons suspected to be suffering from mental crises and falling under this new threshold would be subject to a background check for a history of mental disorder?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, it is unclear to me also what the records refer to and what kind of history would be applicable here.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If there is no history, does this mean that no intervention is possible?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Fourth, given the concerns above, what safeguards, guidelines or training and support would police officers be given in applying the new threshold to situations on the ground, especially after they have made a decision to detain the suspect?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, we are drawing a delicate balance between public safety on the one hand and the proper treatment and approach to those living with mental illness and conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In an article published in JOM last week, Chan Lee Shan, drawing on her own experiences of being arrested while suffering from her first and only episode of psychosis, raised concerns about a person living with mental illness and crises ending up being traumatised by the experience, particularly if they are then treated no differently from a conventional arrest and held in police cells while checks are being made and next steps are being decided as to what would be the most appropriate step for treatment, release or otherwise.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are not theoretical concerns, as after all, the Mah case was one where the officer was found to have made certain statements which were later withdrawn after being contradicted by body-worn camera footage and the judge also expressed concerns about the discrepancies between the medical report produced by the examining doctor and the evidence later submitted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The safeguards and guidelines I asked about are thus extremely important if an occasion arises where the conduct of the arrest or apprehension and subsequent procedures are problematic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Taking a step back to look at a bigger picture and in light of the Second Minister's acknowledgement of Deputy Prime Minister's declaration to this House that mental health is a key national priority, in February 2024 and the large number of Members who spoke to express their concern and even alarm over the situation facing us, I am worried about the amendments to the MHTCTA unnecessarily perpetuating stigma against persons living with mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This entrenchment of discrimination against those living with mental health conditions was also a concern that was highlighted in an op-ed published in The Straits Times last week.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The authors pointed out quite rightly that this is a major concern and identified the balance between three main prongs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, upholding public safety; second, respect for the dignity of the person in crisis; and third, the proportionate use of force.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For sure, this is a tricky balance to get right and I hope that my concerns raised above can help us better appreciate the various segments contained of each of these prongs when discussing whether these amendments help or hinder our stated aims to reduce and ultimately eliminate stigma for those living with mental illness or mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A related point then is also whether the police are best placed to respond to persons experiencing mental health crises.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In recent years, many countries have taken steps to implement alternative strategies to provide support and de-escalate the situation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, in 2017, Sweden introduced a psychiatric emergency response team which would send an ambulance comprising two mental health nurses and one paramedic to attend to persons experiencing a mental health crisis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Another approach is the United Kingdom (UK) Street triage model, a partnership scheme between the police and approved mental health professionals to provide advice and support for people experiencing mental health crises.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have taken encouraging steps in this direction here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In March 2021, IMH partnered SPF to pilot the Crisis Response Team, a mental health crisis response team in Singapore dedicated to providing timely care and support to persons with suicidal tendencies in the community.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such a move can also help reduce the strain on our police.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have to balance our current police and public safety approach to persons experiencing mental health crises and discuss how we may adopt a more person-centric approach that focuses on providing care and support in these situations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I thus conclude my speech with two suggestions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, I hope that more work will be done across the Government to educate and help more citizens better understand the complex issues that lie behind the occasional intersection between public law enforcement and those experiencing mental health crises.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: At the launch of the Collective, former President Halimah Yaacob noted in her speech that we should not erroneously associate criminality or violence with mental health conditions, as this is rarely the case.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We therefore need more public education campaigns to help Singaporeans better appreciate the difficulties involved in achieving the tricky balance between public safety and the needs and dignity of those living with mental health conditions, which may end up being infringed when they are unable to get appropriate support and treatment that is needed to get them and their loved ones when they may be experiencing a mental health crisis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, interested members of the public can be trained as community first responders to support persons experiencing mental health crises.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With their knowledge, these trained volunteers can also serve as ambassadors to educate their communities and persons living with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, local SIM card misuse has seen an exponential surge in recent years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The nature of these scams has also evolved, making them more insidious.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the past, a simple rule of thumb of ignoring unexpected calls with foreign numbers sufficed as a cautionary measure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, criminals have now shifted tactics, exploiting local phone numbers to lure unsuspecting victims.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This shift preys on the inherent trust we place on local calls, especially for our vulnerable elderly population.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our seniors are more likely to answer local calls, creating a prime opportunity for scammers to exploit their trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The consequences can be devastating when victims fall prey to such deception.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I commend the Government's initiative to tighten regulations and combat this issue, I believe that there are several key clarifications that need to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must acknowledge the vulnerability of certain individuals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These very people can become unwitting accomplices, having their SIM cards misused either by mistake or through exploitation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are, in essence, both victims and potential targets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am glad that those who have legitimate reasons or were genuinely tricked into giving up their particulars would not be held liable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, I also understand that this could complicate enforcement and proving intent is always difficult.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hence, we must try to tackle the problem at its roots.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there plans to educate and warn the elderly against the misuse of their identity in SIM card registration?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, how does this Bill address situations where multiple SIM cards have been misused by family members, but the elderly person feigns or alleges ignorance?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be penalties for the elderly and subsequently, the main perpetrator?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, we should create a system that empowers retailers to whistle blow conveniently and anonymously.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The role of retailers in combating this issue cannot be overstated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Empowering them to act as a safeguard is critical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But expecting them to reject every suspected case of bulk SIM card purchases for malicious purposes may not be practical.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Customer service personnel may face pressure from their superiors or irate customers if a purchase is mistakenly flagged.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, exploring alternative avenues for retailers to report suspicious activities is essential.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government should develop an avenue that allows for convenient and anonymous whistle blowing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This would alleviate the burden of direct confrontation for customer service personnel and will encourage more proactive reporting.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, exploring incentives for such reporting is worth considering.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Recognising retailers who actively participate in combating SIM card misuse could be highly effective.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, a public recognition program that designates them as "Trusted SIM Retailers" would not only incentivise vigilance, but also boost their reputation among customers seeking secure and responsible service providers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It may also deter possible perpetrators from approaching such retailers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This approach fosters collaboration and promotes ethical practices within the retail sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, Sir, I will move on to address the amendments relating to the apprehension of mentally disordered persons.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I support the move to empower Police officers to apprehend the said individuals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The harm they may cause to themselves or others around them is irreparable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An obvious example is if they end up successfully committing suicide or homicide.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The move is a pre-emptive approach that protects both the person, as well as those around them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At the outset, we must always remember that mental illness is not a crime.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mental illness expressed as anti-social behaviour in and of itself may not be life-threatening.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even among the mentally ill, there is a wide spectrum of behaviours.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is thus imperative that our Police officers must be better equipped to identify potential signs of mental illness, both in the individuals with a history and those without, always with the view of harm reduction and not the stigmatisation of the mentally ill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am concerned that if our Police officers lack the expertise to do so, they may not be able to use the powers effectively or responsibly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The recent case of Mah Kiat Seng vs Attorney-General and Others has raised some concerns.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this case, Mr Mah claimed he was wrongly arrested and imprisoned based on false information provided by a Police officer.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can the Government prevent similar situations from happening again?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The good standing of our men in blue relies on them being able to exercise their powers in a manner that balances the need for decisive action in high-stress operational situations, with a keen sense of human dignity and skillful instinct honed through experience and training.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is all the more delicate when Police deal with the mentally ill who have already been triggered by stressful situations and this becomes further exacerbated by Police intervention.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Public trust in our institutions hinges on the belief that we act in the best interests of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This extends to our Police force, who require proper training and clear guidelines to uphold their duty effectively.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Unclear procedures create apprehension for both the public and Police officers, potentially hindering enforcement and fostering disputes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The proposed law empowers Police to apprehend individuals under specific circumstances.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To ensure transparency and to minimise apprehension, the Ministry should clarify these thresholds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, clear guidelines are critical to prevent potential power abuses and ensure effective collaboration with mental health professionals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While traditional training methods have value, equipping Police with real-world case studies, hands-on experience and access to mental health experts is vital.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Training should emphasise de-escalation tactics and provide a framework for officers to escalate complex situations to appropriate personnel for further evaluation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moving on, Mr Speaker, Sir, as we delve into other aspects of the Bill, it is critical to acknowledge the limitations of some of the new regulations while exploring further solutions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While section 39H of the Bill allows for extraterritorial effect, the question of enforcement remains.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will we establish collaborative efforts with other foreign jurisdictions to apprehend perpetrators operating outside our borders?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The criteria outlined – cases deemed "not of a serious nature" or with "insufficient grounds" – warrant further clarification.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, how will this impact issues like neighbourly disputes or noise complaints?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will isolated incidents of nuisance be entirely dismissed, leaving residents with no avenue for recourse?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A clear framework for addressing such situations is necessary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Educational initiatives can empower them to identify and prevent such exploitation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A system for anonymous whistleblowing by retailers, coupled with an incentive program like "Trusted SIM Retailer" designation, can significantly improve vigilance and reporting.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, regarding the amendments to Police powers, while empowering officers to apprehend individuals with mental health issues is critical, ensuring fair implementation is paramount.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To this end, transparency and clear guidelines are essential to prevent misuse of power and public fear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We also need to equip Police officers with comprehensive training, with real-world scenarios, giving them access to mental health professionals, and providing a framework to escalate complex cases.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By prioritising these recommendations, we can strengthen the Bill and ensure it safeguards both our citizens and their security.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us work together to send a clear message: zero tolerance for SIM card misuse and having trust in the enforcement of Police powers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the proposed amendments, we can create a more secure Singapore for all.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: My contribution to this debate relates specifically to part 3 of the Bill, the Amendments Relating To Apprehension under the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Act and the Police Force Act.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to declare that I am a psychiatrist in private practice and am the Honorary Secretary of the Singapore Psychiatric Association.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I am also a visiting consultant psychiatrist at a restructured hospital.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to also add that I have dealt with many a psychiatric emergency in my line of work.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I have myself been conflicted and made the harrowing call to law enforcement over grave concerns that an acquaintance was at risk of potential suicide.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The large majority of those with mental illness struggle silently, may appear normal to most and are able to navigate life's challenges with some treatment and support from family and loved ones.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The individuals for whom this Bill could apply represent but a slither of individuals who are afflicted with mental illness or mental health concerns.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: When placed under much duress, entrenched and severe mental illness can impair one's mind, to the extent that he or she may consider life not worth living anymore and contemplate suicide.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Often, at this juncture, all hope appears lost, reasonableness is absent and negative thoughts have festered well beyond fleeting moments of self-doubt in themselves and their lives.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: If we are lucky, such individuals – with encouragement from family and loved ones – would agree to present themselves to a psychiatrist much earlier for treatment.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: However, there are times where family members, who themselves could also be at a loss, reach out for external help from community organisations or call upon law enforcement, especially when they are deeply concerned for the safety of the individual.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I can say with some confidence that our Police officers are confronted with this on a daily basis.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Almost a daily occurrence, at the IMH Emergency Room, ever so often there would be some Police presence bringing a distressed person to be assessed by a designated medical practitioner, on account of section 7 of the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Act, or MHCTA.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: When someone is on the brink of suicide and immense despair, they would have lost all hope, are taxed with a sense of worthlessness and with no longing to continue living.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Police officers and their Home Team colleagues remain their last hope for rescue, and such officers often put themselves at risk to honour their duty to protect fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: For context, often these apprehensions take place in unfamiliar surroundings and home environments, in the presence of sharp objects like blades and knives, with open ungrilled windows or even at corridors of significant height.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The tension in the air would be palpable, sometimes with raised voices of frustration and emotions running high.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Even as I advocate for this Bill today, there are three things I hope the Ministry can look into moving forward, if not already done today, to really reassure concerns on the ground and hon Members of the House today.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Such structured training would also be important to ensure that while there is some latitude and range for judgement by Police officers on the ground, the exercise of such powers of apprehension continues to be done with propriety, with confidence and with safety in mind.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Second, to ensure access to psychiatric evaluation and assessment without delay after apprehension.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: If the premise of the apprehension was due to concerns over a potential suicide attempt and a mental disorder, then it follows that it is treatment that the individual needs and care and assessment must be forthcoming as soon as safety is established.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Third, to work more closely with mental health professionals in such crisis work.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: As a clinician and psychiatrist, my role in addressing psychiatric emergencies is moot without first ensuring that any patient of mine is safe, first and foremost.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: No meaningful medical treatment is possible without first ensuring safety of the patient and rescuer.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This parallels our approach to dealing with medical emergencies too, as is the protocol for Basic Cardiac Life Support which I am sure many Members of the House are trained and are familiar with.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The acronym is DRSABCD – Assess for Danger, Assess for Responsiveness, Send for Help, Airway, Breathing, CPR and Defibrillation, where in the first instance, danger must be ameliorated as a first and utmost priority and remains several steps ahead before CPR treatment can take place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: By now, we are all well aware of how the proliferation of scams and cybercrimes and hence, the overall crime rate in Singapore is on a sharp rise in recent years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While we may not be living in the metaverse per se as yet, our digital lives and online footprint are increasingly inescapable aspects of our everyday lives – from the way we communicate and socialise via online messaging apps and social media, the way we go about our daily jobs in front of our laptops and even the way we transact in the offline world buying lunch or groceries, with Singapore moving closer towards a cashless society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Gallup's Law and Order Index uses four questions to gauge people's sense of personal security and their own experiences with crime and law enforcement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While much of these relate to one's sense of physical safety and security, in this day and age, it is worth looking at these questions from the digital sphere as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, one of the questions relate to, "within the last 12 months, have you had money or property stolen from you or another household member?" These days, the losses from scams are likely to be way more significant, sometimes involving our life savings, than losing one's wallet from snatch theft or robbery.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And while we may "feel safe walking alone at night", it is noteworthy that 96% of the population, aged 15 and above, are at least somewhat concerned about becoming a victim of scams; with 99% of seniors, aged 60 and above, sharing the same concern.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As scammers and criminal networks continue to evolve their approach in committing scams and cybercrimes against Singaporeans, we need to step up our game to reverse the worrying trend in scam cases and I believe the new measures would be a welcome addition into our arsenal in the war against scammers and cybercriminals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Nonetheless, I have a few areas of concern which I hope the Minister will be able to address.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Bill introduces offences targeting three groups of offenders – irresponsible registrants; those receiving, supplying or possessing local SIM cards; and retailers facilitating fraudulent registration of local SIM cards.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given our earlier efforts to tighten SIM card registration requirements and the implementation of the +65 prefix to identify foreign scam syndicates spoofing local numbers, these scammers have turned to using local SIM cards instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As set out in the MHA's press release, the rampant misuse of local SIM cards to perpetuate scams has been driven by people who give away their SIM cards or provide their particulars to others to be used to sign up for SIM cards, typically for money, also known as "irresponsible registrants".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While it certainly is irresponsible of such people when viewed from a rational third-party perspective, it may be the case of ignorance from the perspective of certain persons, of the significant harms such a seemingly innocent move can cause.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To me, it is much less defensible to feign ignorance when it comes to cases involving lending one's identity to be a phantom employee, even earning extra Central Provident Fund (CPF) along the way, while enabling dishonest companies to sidestep foreign worker quotas, or to wilfully lend one's bank accounts in return for a fee to facilitate money laundering.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To what extent do we wish to pursue or even imprison an elderly person, or someone who may not be literate or sophisticated enough to see the criminal element of this act, even as someone gave him a "token sum" to thank him for his time and efforts and would have "ticked the box" on receiving "any gain"?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What kind of educational or information campaigns will be conducted to protect those who may not have wilfully committed an offence for a quick buck and could now face imprisonment?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   As we all know, while physical crimes have decreased over the past five years, scams and cybercrime cases have risen sharply, leading to increase in the overall crime rate in Singapore in recent years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Signs indicate that more scammers are using local SIM cards for scams and illegal lending, even setting up accounts such as PayNow to receive illicit funds and creating accounts on messaging apps such as WhatsApp.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He was frequently at our MPS and we learnt of his many challenges as he grew to trust us and confide in us.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: N was in his 60s and I believe him to be an undiagnosed special needs adult, a high-functioning one capable of independent living, albeit an awkward one when it comes to relationships and social norms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During one of our MPS, he came distraught and shared that he was arrested by the Police recently.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He had ordered fast food delivery to be sent to his mother, who is living in an aged home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When his mother told him that she did not receive the delivery, he charged down to the local fast food restaurant, demanding to be compensated for the food his family had failed to receive.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: N is a tall man and when he is angry, he talks in a very loud voice and can be quite intimidating for the uninitiated.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Needless to say, our local fast food counter staff was ill-equipped to deal with him and she called in the mall security and the local Police team for assistance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That day, according to N, he caused the rather elderly security guard to fall.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He pushed a passerby who came in to help and he nearly fell on a policeman.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He was subsequently taken in by the Police.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When N recounted the event to me, he was distraught but thankful that he did not cause more harm to the people involved.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He still wanted his fast food delivered, which was why he came to see us at the MPS, but acknowledged that he would be in deeper trouble, or perhaps have even injured himself seriously, should there not be intervention by the Police.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While N's situation is perhaps an extreme one, we see semblances of this in our everyday lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, when someone on the public transport has a meltdown, Singaporeans do not often react kindly.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More often than not, the commuters would give them a dirty look, or exchange disapproving looks with their fellow commuters, if not simply resigning to "mind their own businesses".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It goes without saying, that the social rejection does not help someone who is already over-sensitised.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If our commuters could react to the meltdown with some understanding and compassion, very much like if during that period, N had been treated with some empathy and understanding, the commuter and N would have a much easier time coaching themselves to calm down.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have full support that this conviction will continue its work beyond the matter of enforcement in time to come.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The October 2023 report and the February 2024 Motion collectively brought tremendous encouragement to anyone and everyone with interest and concern with mental health and wellness.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Persons in recovery, caregivers, mental health professionals and service providers – all found comfort, fresh hope and renewed expectations.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: When I first read this proposed Law Enforcement and Other Matters Bill – specifically in the reference to mental health and also read the resulting media comment, I was alarmed and concerned.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Why the need to make the change now just as we are building a national collective toward enhanced mental health support?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Plugging gaps in the law is the task of the Government.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill is wide-ranging and mental health is just one of many proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I have no issue with the other amendments proposed in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Could this amendment relating to mental health have been introduced at another time?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This would enable the many follow-up aspects from the October 2023 Ministry of Health (MOH) strategy plan and the February 2024 Parliamentary Motion to settle in and gain traction.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Would we not be a better prepared community having given this bit more time?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Can we still consider deferring this if we are truly trying to send a positive signal of hope for persons coping with mental health issues, especially while we are doing all we can to encourage more to come forward and seek help early and while we continue to fight the stigma associated with mental health?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This House is likely to be aware of several articles that have since been written about the Bill.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Most of these articles expressed varying degrees of concerns on the proposed amendments and have been written by persons in recovery, by caregivers and by mental healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Ms Chan is a patient advocate, an author and a person with lived experience.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I met Ms Chan some years back and heard her story of recovery.
