speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we do not have many individuals like Ms Chan Li Shan, who have documented their journeys of recovery.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I have also heard mental health professionals expressing the need for more persons in recovery to write of their experiences so we can better understand this from the perspective of one receiving treatment and care, understand the challenges, appreciate their feelings and emotions and recognise that just like everyone else, persons in recovery are fellow human beings who have views, who can feel hurt and rejection and can appreciate care and affection.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Today, mental health care at the patient level has improved.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Individuals, such as Ms Chan, have shared about the pain and trauma in the use of restraints in hospitals.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In her article she voices the issue of real risk of trauma on individuals in recovery if the law is not applied in the way it may be intended.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: She concludes with these words, "Mental illness is not a crime and our laws should not be constructed to make it so.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I object." Ms Sabrina Ooi, CEO of Calm Collective Asia, also shared her experience on the trauma of getting arrested.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: She calls on us to find compassion to look beyond the surface and to broaden our perspective on what it means to keep our society safe from the mentally disordered.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Dr Jonathan Kuek, clinical mental health researcher, raised the concern on the thresholds for apprehension.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Can the hon Minister give reasonable assurance to persons in recovery and their caregivers and families, that degrees of unusual or undesirable behaviour can be sufficiently calibrated before apprehension is deemed necessary?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Ms Porsche Poh, Executive Director of Silver Ribbon, wrote on ensuring that police are competent in managing mental health crises.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The concerns are not questioning the integrity and existing capabilities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Many give credit for the thoughtful and professional way our law enforcement officers execute their roles.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I sought the views of Mr Nicholas Lee, Executive Director of Resilience Collective, a mental health charity powered by peers for peers.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Peers are persons in recovery and persons with lived experience.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Lee shared this with me, "When I first heard the news of enhancing our police officers' powers when making arrests of people with mental health conditions, I immediately felt there would be a reintroduction of stigma on mental health. 'Why would normal powers not be enough?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: These potentially new perceptions are not healthy for us as we have been slowly chipping away at this huge, seemingly insurmountable, boulder called stigma." I have read briefly that law enforcement agencies would send officers for training.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: While I applaud this, I am concerned how thorough this training would be.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I say this because each person is different and triggers may take very different forms.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As a person being subject to such an arrest, one must always remember that emotions will be at play and whether or not I can control my emotions.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The law, I agree, is meant for good.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: But perhaps, what is needed is a joint effort to develop these methods so that both officers and persons with mental health conditions are protected.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: A group with representation from all – from the Police, psychiatrists, mental health professionals and persons with mental health conditions – so that no one is left behind or not considered.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Ms Anthea Ong, former Nominated Member of Parliament; Ms Cassandra Chia, President of the Disabled People's Association; and Dr Rayner Tan from the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health penned an article entitled, "When someone has a mental health crisis, arrest is not the answer".

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: They too speak up for the persons facing mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We do have specialised response teams for mental health.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The challenge would be to differentiate the correct response when a call for help or action is received.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As with the issue faced by our Accidents and Emergency (A&E) departments as a first port of call for any semblance of a health emergency, so will calls to the police be a likely default position for disruptive behaviour.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to refer the commentary written by SG Mental Health Matters.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Concerns expressed here relate to the significant discretion handed to Police officers.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There is also the concern about the potential resultant trauma on persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Dr Jared Ng's commentary, "Expanded police powers don't have to mean 'three steps forward, two steps back' for mental health in Singapore", looks at the differing views and offers this proposal: "Mental health professionals and law enforcement officers have a responsibility to work together to ensure the best possible outcomes.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: A multi-stakeholder committee could give and gather feedback on operational processes, evaluate intervention strategies to inform policy adjustments.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Only then can we ensure both public safety and the compassionate treatment of those in mental health crises.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: What matters now, is how stakeholders are engaged and collaborate so that Singapore does not detract from the strides made in mental healthcare." Dr Ng was chief of emergency and crisis care at IMH and therefore a voice with experience.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: He speaks on the interface between the Police and mental health and cites some collaborative models from the United States, the Nordic countries and Australia.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Several years ago, I was introduced to the value of response teams which included trained peers, or persons with a lived experience, as part of the team.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: A person with a lived experience may often be better at communicating with another person facing similar challenges.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: They may be better equipped in helping to de-escalate certain situations.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I would suggest that should a multi-stakeholder committee be considered, we need to include persons with lived experience as mentioned by Mr Lee from Resilience Collective.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: With a troubled mind, I consulted psychiatrist Dr Muni Winslow for his advice and guidance.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Since the release of the Second Reading of the Bill, Dr Winslow has received calls of concern from his community.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to share Dr Winslow's views and this is with his permission: "I think the key drawback is that most police knowledge is no better than a layman.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It would be helpful if all public-facing police personnel get at least some basic training in identifying symptoms of mental illness – the different types – as it will help them in de-escalating violence, for example, alcoholism and domestic violence and so forth; and identifying signs of dangerousness in folks with mental conditions.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: They should continue to be free to enjoy public outings and all forms of suitable recreation as citizens.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: They may have a teenager, young or older adult with autism and we are all familiar that in some instances meltdowns happen.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, persons with certain other conditions may also find themselves under greater scrutiny just because they exhibit behaviour different from what society perceives as the norm?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We must not be seen to have taken three steps forward only to take two steps backwards.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Jeffery Tan, CEO of Mindset Care Limited, a charity established to make a tangible difference to the Singapore mental health community, had this to share with me, "To borrow the phrase from Professor Tommy Koh, as a 'loving Singaporean critic', we often 'overengineer' solution to situations.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In so doing, we have the tendency to inordinately apply more 'head logic' than 'heart logic'.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: If it is eminently clear that the person is struggling under a mental illness, it begs the question whether arresting the individual will offer any valuable solution to the situation at hand and more importantly, the individual.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We do not need more 'head logic', which is arrest and apprehension, in this proposed change.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As a maturing society that seeks to more inclusive, there is need for us to have greater tolerance, understanding, compassion and a clear demonstration of heart and not just head.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The maintenance of public safety and order is important for the community.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: But this cannot be at the expense of those in the community that will need our help and support – the weak, the vulnerable, the mentally unwell." Mr Tan concludes with this question: is it possible that the proposed change in the law is not addressing the real issues that need to be focused on?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I see a silver lining because we have seen many from across the mental health sector come forward and speak up.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: All these voices bring us better understanding as a community, greater public awareness, hopefully, with more care and compassion and understanding and resulting in overall improvement in our support systems.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This will lead us closer to normalising mental health and wellness.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I see a sliver lining because we all now know that trauma in recovery is something we must prevent.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I see a silver lining because the elephant in the room can be debated for the benefit of all who continue to suffer in silence.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I see a silver lining as persons in recovery will be given every opportunity and every support to do so at their own pace and with respect.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Many concerns have been raised, many questions have been asked.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The hon Minister has also given some background and clarifications in the introduction of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I have added some additional specific questions for the hon Minister to kindly address and clarify.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I continue to be unsettled when I think of the possible undesirable consequences of this Bill on individuals in our society.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I also acknowledge the Minister will need to give equal assurance to the public and continue to give unwavering support to the excellent work of the Home Team.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They have been a topic of passionate discussion and I wish to convey some concerns and seek clarifications on behalf of those we serve.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we debate these amendments, we need to ensure that these changes enable our police officers to effectively discharge their duties while providing care and support for individuals struggling with mental health issues, as well as their loved ones and caregivers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am concerned about the treatment of individuals who have been apprehended.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These individuals are often in a vulnerable state, and it is imperative that we treat them with kindness and empathy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can the Minister provide clarity on the procedures in place for their rehabilitation and treatment?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How do we further improve these processes to ensure better outcomes for these individuals, providing them with the support and care that they need during these difficult times?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moreover, I would like to inquire about the follow-up mechanisms with psychiatric institutions and social services.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ensuring continuity of care is essential for the holistic well-being of such individuals and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The term "reasonable" is subjective and can vary from one situation to another.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the other hand, any ambiguity could force officers to hastily assess individuals' mental health, placing an unfair burden on them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our officers must be adequately trained and supported to help them navigate these complex scenarios with compassion and discernment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Training our officers in active listening and de-escalation techniques can enable them to interact with individuals experiencing mental health crises with greater empathy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, an officer equipped with these skills can more effectively assist someone having a panic attack in public, using non-threatening body language and a gentle tone to offer support and guide the individual to appropriate help.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In other jurisdictions, there is a growing understanding of the importance of collaboration between law enforcement agencies and mental health professionals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These collaborative approaches between the two entities seek to integrate mental health expertise into police responses, prioritise the well-being of individuals in crisis, and reduce reliance on punitive measures.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Advancing community mental health support will also mean increased support for Police Officers and downstream care for individuals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A more collaborative approach between law enforcement and mental health professionals is essential to prioritise the well-being of individuals in crisis.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Specialised Crisis Intervention Team (CIT) programmes, like those in some jurisdictions, train officers to de-escalate mental health crises and connect individuals with services than resorting to arrest or apprehension.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Research shows CIT improves officer attitudes and reduces injuries during crisis calls.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some Australian states employ unified teams of police and mental health professionals for specialised crisis responses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am sure that the Ministry has considered some of the models for adaptation in our context and considered the challenges.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addressing these challenges, enhancing upstream structural interactions between community mental health teams and Neighbourhood Police Centres (NPCs) is crucial for better coordination of responses and support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, is the Ministry exploring models for fostering deeper collaboration in this regard?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, our front-line police officers, including younger National Servicemen, are often the first responders to incidents involving individuals in mental health crises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Witnessing such situations can take a significant emotional toll on them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Police Psychological Services Department (PPSD) offers a multi-faceted approach for officers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Dedicated para counsellors are present in all Police units and departments, while PPSD psychologists and Home Team psychiatrists offer professional in-house counselling.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In line with these amendments, what more can we do to ensure our front-line officers’ mental health is taken care of?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, the decriminalisation of suicide was a significant legislative reform aimed at recognising mental health issues as medical concerns rather than criminal acts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have received feedback expressing concerns about how this amendment aligns with the decriminalisation of suicide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Notably, the Bill strives to enhance our nation's ability to combat scams, strengthen the effectiveness of Home Team operations, and ensure the seamless functioning of Yellow Ribbon Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While I acknowledge the objectives and benefits of these amendments, I have some clarifications and suggestions that I will now discuss.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Before I do so, I would like to declare my current role as the Head of the Public Safety and Security Programme at Singapore University of Social Sciences and have previously worked as a Probation Officer for the Ministry of Social and Family Development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: They are designed to bolster our defence against fraudulent activities and provide our law enforcement agencies with more robust mechanisms to tackle this evolving threat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By doing so, we are not only safeguarding the financial well-being of our citizens but also upholding the integrity of our nation's economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This malicious practice, where cybercriminals pose as legitimate entities, is a growing risk that threatens the operation of many organisations in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: An important question that we must ask ourselves is, how do we equip our employees to recognise and avoid such at?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: One potential answer lies in real-life simulations that mimic phishing scenarios.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By providing employees with these scenarios, we enable them to understand the tactics of cybercriminals and equip them with the necessary skills to identify and avoid phishing attempts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The quality of the training materials and the competence of the trainers play a vital role in the effectiveness of this experiential training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I will now turn my attention to the proposed amendments outlined in section 14D, which would exempt responsibility for transmitting a message that is false or fabricated for the legitimate purpose of raising public awareness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On one hand, it could aid in spreading awareness about phishing and other cyber threats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, it could potentially be misused by individuals with malicious intent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I welcome the introduction of Part 6A.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These rules are indeed a significant step towards deterring the misuse of local SIM cards and I commend the Ministry for their proactive approach in addressing this issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate the safeguard in place as these offences are not used against those who are genuinely unaware of the unlawful act or those who are tricked into registration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This shows the Ministry's commitment to fairness and justice, and this is an important measure in protecting those who are manipulated into acquiring a SIM card or those who may not be aware that their action is illegal in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is, however, important that we continue to monitor the situation closely and make necessary adjustments to ensure that this rule remains effective in preventing scams.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: And what resources, including training, are being provided to general Home Team officers to increase their capacity to recognise, investigate and prosecute scams?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, with regards to section 39H, how does the Ministry work with telecommunication organisations and enforcement agencies outside of Singapore to prevent, investigate and prosecute scams?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome these amendments, noting the high likelihood of bad actors using corporations and associations as a façade to conduct unlawful and criminal activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that note, I would like to clarify: what legislative provisions exist to hold individuals personally liable for scams perpetrated by individuals or entities for whom they are administratively or legally responsible?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Our Police force and law enforcement agencies work tirelessly to ensure the safety and security of our nation and its people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, to effectively carry out their duties, they require legislative support that is responsive to the evolving nature of security challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed amendments will provide our Home Team with the necessary legal framework to optimise their operations, streamline processes and enhance coordination between various agencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This will undoubtedly result in a more efficient and cohesive approach towards maintaining law and order, as well as responding swiftly to emerging threats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Being efficient is one pillar of law and order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While I recognise the importance of this measure in protecting the public, it is essential to consider the potential drawbacks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Police are not mental health professionals and their interactions with individuals experiencing mental health crises can be complex and challenging.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The use of this power must be balanced with the need to respect individual rights and dignity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: There are several arguments against police apprehending mentally ill individuals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, as highlighted by the Minister earlier, the purpose of section 13 is to authorise the detention of people living with mental illness to prevent harm that these individuals may inflict on others or themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, to prevent a criminal act and to provide for their treatment and care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This includes understanding the signs of a mental health crisis, developing specialised responses and learning how to de-escalate situations effectively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that note, I seek clarifications on the following issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed amendments grant Police officers the authority to pursue individuals who have attempted suicide and are failing to stop, to be assisted by police.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, it permits any person to apprehend such individuals, emphasising the collective responsibility to prevent suicide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I support this change, but it is crucial to examine potential challenges associated with this amendment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: First and foremost, let us acknowledge the significance of this amendment in addressing the pressing issue of suicide prevention.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By allowing Police officers to pursue individuals attempting suicide, we enhance our capacity to intervene promptly and provide the necessary support and assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, empowering others to apprehend individuals in distress underscores the importance of community involvement in suicide prevention efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This collective responsibility emphasises that every individual has a role to play in safeguarding the well-being of others.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is, however, important that we approach the matter with sensitivity and understanding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Suicidal ideation is a complex and deeply personal struggle, often stemming from underlying mental health issues and emotional distress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, we must ensure that our actions are guided by empathy and compassion – recognising the vulnerability of those experiencing suicidal thoughts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, while the intention behind this amendment is to prevent harm and provide support, there is a risk of unintended consequences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Pursuing individuals who have attempted suicide may exacerbate feelings of distress and increase the likelihood of further harm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is imperative to implement safeguards and measures to mitigate these risks and ensure that interventions are conducted with the utmost care and consideration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure the successful implementation of this amendment, several measures must be put in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, protocols should be established to guide the appropriate response and intervention, taking into account the mental health and well-being of the individual in distress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, efforts should be made to enhance mental health support services and resources, ensuring that individuals in crisis have access to the help they need.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This includes increasing awareness of available support networks and promoting destigmatisation of mental health issues within our society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to share an initiative rolled out in Australia called Police, Ambulance and Clinician Early Response (PACER).

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is a collaborative effort with the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) Ambulance Service and Canberra Health Services to enhance mental health crisis response.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: PACER offers a more comprehensive approach by deploying a team consisting of a paramedic, clinician and police officer, to address the needs of the most vulnerable mental health patients.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that note, I would like to clarify: would the Ministry consider such partnerships and inter-agency cooperation to ensure positive outcomes for individuals with mental illness or disorder?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider recruiting suitably qualified volunteers, including those with qualifications in psychology, counselling and social work, to enhance the provision of support to people living with mental illness?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, as we move forward, let us remember the importance of approaching this issue with empathy, understanding and sensitivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Together, we can create a society where every individual feels supported, valued and empowered to seek help when they need it most.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Before I conclude, I would like to share some words from Deputy Prime Minister Wong’s Motion on Advancing Mental Health on 7 February 2024, “We need to do more to destigmatise mental health conditions, so that people do not hesitate to seek help.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Stigma reduces a complex and difficult problem into unhelpful labels or stereotypes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It opens people struggling with mental health to discrimination, such as in the job market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It may cause them to be socially ostracised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It makes them feel ashamed, isolated and stops them from seeking treatment.” Mr Speaker, clarifications notwithstanding, I support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Although it represents a small segment of the Bill, it has drawn much attention within the mental health community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we navigate the complexities of mental health and the pivotal role of law enforcement in our community, it is imperative to recognise the delicate balance required in addressing such sensitive issues.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My experience as a Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) officer handling suicide calls has significantly influenced my perspective for today.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I recall the urgency and the critical decisions that need to be made in split seconds, because lives are at stake.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These experiences have taught me an invaluable lesson.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Behind every call is a human being in need, a family in despair and a family waiting for an officer's safe return.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With this understanding, I approach the amendments proposed in the Bill, striving to highlight the balance that protects all that are involved; those experiencing the crisis and the officers responding with the hope of making a positive impact.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The amendments proposed under the Bill seek to refine and clarify law enforcement's powers when responding to individuals experiencing mental health crises.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This initiative underscores our commitment to enhancing public safety while preserving the dignity and well-being of those in vulnerable states.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Last week, I had a dialogue with mental health advocates, including Total Wellness Initiative, Calm Collective, Silver Ribbon Society, Singapore Association for Mental Health, Mental Act and even PERGAS, where they raised concerns and sought to understand the Bill better.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: There is an apprehension that, without careful implementation, these amendments could inadvertently contribute to the stigma surrounding mental health or lead to discrimination.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This fear is not unfounded; that in our pursuit of safety, it is possible that we may overlook the necessity for understanding and respect towards those experiencing mental health issues.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They highlighted stories and studies pointing to the potential for increased anxiety and trauma stemming from such interventions or interactions, advocating for response mechanisms that are not only effective but also empathetic and respectful.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With the new tier system, we could have a different approach to addressing apprehension processes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a misunderstanding between apprehension and arrest – apprehension and arrest – and understanding the scope of the proposed amendments.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, some thought the proposed amendments would give Police officers the power to search and restrain apprehended subjects, similar to when arresting criminal suspects.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Also, there is a misunderstanding that the amendments will impact the decriminalisation of suicides or impact the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Act and change the approach or processes that the Police may take in apprehending a person with a mental health condition.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The consensus from the dialogue is that, such misunderstandings must be clarified and communicated clearly and the public must be aware of them, too, as the spread of such misunderstandings can be detrimental in our efforts to destigmatise mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, I am glad that the Minister elaborated in her Reading earlier and gave clear examples of how we aim to solve these problems.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our Police force plays a critical role in ensuring the safety and security of our community, a duty that extends into the complex realm of mental health and it is not easy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The proposed amendments are about striking a balance; ensuring that our officers have the clarity and guidance they need to make compassionate decisions in the heat of the moment, which could save lives as well.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And on that point, I also note that there are proposals about having a team to go along with the Police officers and my experience tells me that sometimes we do not have the luxury of time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It could take seconds or minutes or even hours and that is when a team could be possible.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But usually, the decisions need to be made in a split second and I do not envy the challenges that our Police officers and other Home Team officers face.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the handling of attempted suicide cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The media has reported on how the Police is working with the IMH crisis response team for cases where there are signs of attempted suicide by calling a dedicated IMH hotline to conduct a suicide risk assessment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Police also has a Crisis Negotiation Unit to handle attempted suicide cases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share the Police's process for dealing with an attempted suicide case, including the involvement of the IMH crisis response team and the Crisis Negotiation Unit?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At what point will the Police apprehend a person reasonably suspected to be about to commit suicide?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What training is provided to officers to handle attempted suicide cases and to apprehend a person involved in an attempted suicide case?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under the section 26AA(5), every person is bound to help an authorised Police officer in apprehending a person, the Police officer is authorised to apprehend.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the nature of this obligation imposed on a person “bound to help”?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the consequences if the person “bound to help” refuses to provide help?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is a layperson expected to know of their obligation to help and, if so, what steps will be taken to communicate to laypersons that they are obliged to help?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, can Minister also explain, practically speaking, how a person requested to help should determine whether the Police is authorised or not to apprehend a person?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, my second point is on the apprehension of mentally disordered persons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some have raised concerns that we may be over-reliant on the Police in cases of mental health crisis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One alternative that has been raised is that mental health professionals should lead the emergency response in such cases, where possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the city of Eugene, Oregon, crisis counsellors from a community programme called Crisis Assistance Helping Out On The Streets or CAHOOTS, receive hundreds of hours of training and send responders to 3% to 8% of police calls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if Police officers responding to cases of mental health crisis could be accompanied, where possible, by a mental health professional or someone with specialist training?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, we have Victim Care Officers who are specially trained to work with the Police to support victims of crime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it be possible to similarly train specialist community-first responders to support the Police in responding to cases involving individuals with mental health conditions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As for the Police officers, I understand that they are trained to handle persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, the Bill now requires a Police officer to assess if there is sufficient basis for the reasonable suspicion that a conduct is attributable to a mental disorder before apprehending a person.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a different skillset from handling a person with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what training will be provided to Police officers to assess whether the threat of physical harm is attributable to a mental disorder?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry explained in a press release that a person may be traced in Police's records to have a history of mental disorder.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what other records are available to the Police in determining whether the threat of physical harm is attributable to a mental disorder?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, does the Police have access to records maintained by IMH or other medical institutions?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, can the Minister share what steps will be taken after the individual has been apprehended?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, will the person be referred for immediate treatment for the mental disorder?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, are the medical institutions ready for the potential increase in these referrals?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is there a possibility of the person being released back into the community instead of being referred for immediate treatment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, how will the Police assess whether the person is suitable for release back into the community?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is on the new SIM-card related offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These offences target irresponsible or fraudulent registration, transfer and possession of SIM cards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate that the new offences target a set of conduct that is facilitating the growing social problem of scams.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the ways of using technology for wrongdoings are constantly evolving.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Constantly introducing new offences in order to tackle specific methods and technologies if unchecked may lead to an extensive, fragmented and unwieldy set of criminal laws.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may be difficult for the layperson to keep track of and understand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just last year, we amended the Computer Misuse Act and the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act to introduce new offences involving the use of Singpass credentials.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Existing Penal Code provisions on abetment or conspiracy may potentially be broad enough to cover some of the new SIM-card related offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, the Bill introduces new offences of providing a person's personal information to register a SIM card that the person knows will be used to commit an offence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such conduct may potentially be covered under the existing provisions for abetment or conspiracy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They raised many relevant questions which I will try my best to respond to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, those on the new SIM card offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng asked why MHA is introducing new offences, instead of relying on existing laws.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The limitation of the current law is that for irresponsible subscribers and middlemen who deal in local SIM cards, we would need to prove that they had intended to abet an offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But proving intent is incredibly difficult and often impossible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Take the example I mentioned in my opening speech, where a middleman purchased over 1,000 prepaid SIM cards that were fraudulently registered and sent them to persons in Malaysia who used them for scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When he was questioned, he claimed that he merely dealt with the SIM cards and did not know that the receiving parties were scammers or that they would use the SIM cards to commit scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It might indeed be that he did not know, because he did not care to know who bought the SIM cards from him and what they would do with it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is equally difficult to prove criminal conspiracy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is no good reason for such acts, because there are legitimate ways to buy and sell SIM cards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But clearly, there is value to avoid such options and we should not accept them being passed off as legitimate economic activities, when, in fact, they are used to cause harms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As for errant retailers, there is no specific offence under today's laws for fraudulent registration.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While the Police may use other laws to prosecute such retailers, such as offences under the Penal Code or Computer Misuse Act, circumstances of each case may not allow us to proceed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As a result, under today's regime, most errant retailers simply lose their contract with the mobile service provider, effectively getting away scot-free with the profits they had made from the fraudulent registrations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Louis Chua raised concerns about people who exploit elderly persons to obtain SIM cards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the example given by Mr Yip, where an elderly person's particulars are misused by family members or caregivers to register for SIM cards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The elderly person would not be liable for an offence, if we find that he had no reasonable grounds to believe that his particulars would be used to register for SIM cards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police recognise that there are indeed situations where the elderly might have been tricked into sharing their particulars.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police will investigate such cases comprehensively and consider any credible evidence that the elderly person was unaware about how his particulars would be used.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Attorney-General's Chambers will also carefully consider each case on its own facts and circumstances and will only pursue prosecution if there is public interest to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the other hand, the individual who had misused the elderly person's particulars could be liable for an offence of supplying or selling the SIM cards registered in another person's particulars.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, if the individual had pretended to be the elderly person and had used his particulars to sign up for a SIM card without his permission, the individual could also be liable for an offence of cheating by personation under section 416 of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Louis Chua asked if there are plans to educate the elderly population about the misuse of their particulars for SIM card registrations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng shared his concern about the proliferation of laws which are too complicated to understand.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is something that a lot of my colleagues in law enforcement wish they could do in their systems.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But it has been very difficult for them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It would indeed be better and we agree with Mr Louis Ng, if we could streamline these laws.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But at this point in time, this is not a luxury we can afford when scam tactics are still evolving so quickly and Police resources are so stretched.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a trade-off Parliament must consider, whether to prioritise the streamlining of laws or quickly putting in place levers to act against the scammers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we asked victims, their answer would be clear.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I believe we should, in Parliament, similarly accept this trade-off for now.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During these six months, we will step up public education efforts to raise awareness of the new offences, red flags that the public ought to be wary about and measures they can adopt to prevent the misuse of their SIM cards and particulars.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also work with mobile service providers to educate retailers about the new offences and emphasise the penalties that they will face should they be convicted of fraudulent registration.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For the offences of receiving, supplying or possessing SIM cards, Mr Desmond Choo asked how we decided on the threshold of 11 or more SIM cards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Setting a low threshold is therefore important for deterrence from hoarding local SIM cards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, we have also tried to ensure that most law-abiding people are not affected.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A typical person is therefore very unlikely to be holding on to more than 10 SIM cards which are registered in his own name and should not even be in possession of cards not registered in his own name.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, this amendment is not a concern for legitimate subscribers, even if they have more than 10 cards, as they will not be involved in crime.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Desmond Choo suggested imposing minimum fines and imprisonment terms, as well as pegging fines for retailers to a proportion of their annual revenue.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We assess that the proposed penalties are adequate for now.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We do not intend to impose a minimum penalty, so as to give the Courts more flexibility to decide on the appropriate punishment based on the severity of the case.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While fines might be a mere slap on the wrists for large retailers, the possibility of an imprisonment term of up to three years should act as a sufficiently strong deterrent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Razwana and Mr Louis Chua asked about the legislative provisions to hold key officers and senior management liable for offences committed by entities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These include officers who were involved in making the executive decision to commit the offence, as well as those who failed to take reasonable steps to prevent an offence that they knew was going to be committed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members also gave suggestions on preventing the abuse of local SIM cards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Chua asked if mobile service providers might also be liable if they are appointed to retailers, conduct fraudulent registrations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under the new laws, mobile service providers will be liable for an offence, if they were directly involved conducting or facilitating the fraudulent registrations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, we can also take regulatory action against mobile service providers, if we find that they fail to ensure their appointed retailers comply with IMDA's requirements on SIM card registrations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked how we are working with online platforms, such as Telegram.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police have been working with online platforms to take down accounts involved in scams and other crimes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, under today's laws, it is not a crime to go online to buy and sell local SIM cards second-hand.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This means that there are actually no legal grounds to request the platforms to take down accounts involved in such sales of SIM cards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Choo suggested simplifying and standardising the process for a person to authorise another person to register for SIM cards on his behalf.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To clarify, IMDA only allows persons to register for SIM cards under their own names, using their own particulars.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To ensure this, retailers are required to check the identity of the subscriber during the registration process.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mobile service providers may be in breach of their regulatory obligations, should their appointed retailers fail to conduct such checks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If a person wishes to register SIM cards for his family members, he can do so using his own particulars.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip suggested creating an avenue to allow retailers to report suspicious activity conveniently and anonymously.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Retailers can file a Police report, which can be done online conveniently using Singpass.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They can also submit information through the I-Witness online portal, which can be done anonymously.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked about training and other resources given to Home Team officers, including Anti-Scam Command officers, to recognise, investigate and prosecute scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To clarify, the key difficulty we face today is with prosecuting scammers, and the people who help them, including SIM card mules.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today’s amendments will help our police officers successfully take to task the SIM card mules that they arrest.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Razwana also asked how we could work with the telcos to prevent scams.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These have been shared earlier in my opening speech, so I suggest not to belabour the point.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Razwana and Mr Yip asked if we would work with foreign law enforcement agencies to take down scammers operating overseas.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The new SIM card offences will also give the Police more grounds to work with foreign law enforcement agencies to arrest and investigate overseas scammers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In relation to the proposed amendment to section 14D of the MOA, Assoc Prof Razwana asked if the Ministry would consider encouraging entities to undertake simulated phishing exercises using the Cyber Security Agency's (CSA’s) recently published Playbook for the Conduct of Phishing Simulation Exercises.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I earlier noted, such exercises are useful tools for organisations to be better prepared against cybersecurity incidents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked what strategies are in place to prevent people from being misled by genuine cybersecurity warnings and advice.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If her concern is that bad actors could take advantage of the proposed exception to section 14D, let me assure her that we have designed the exception carefully.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not enough for someone to simply claim that they have a legitimate purpose in sending the false message – there is an objective standard that must be met.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Furthermore, malicious actors who seek to exploit this exception, for example, by masquerading as public authorities, will be caught under the existing Penal Code offences like cheating by personation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will now deal with the questions and suggestions on the handling of cases involving persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hear all the Members and your concerns, and it is important to reiterate that this Government is fully committed to advancing mental health.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We recognise that persons with mental health conditions are part of our society and we should do our best to help them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy outlines the whole-of-society approach that we are taking to address this important issue and there are many components of them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members were concerned about social stigma that mental health patients may face and the appropriate care, which we fully understand and agree with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, we are actively working towards destigmatising mental health conditions, so that people do not hesitate to seek help.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Please be assured that Police does not seek to put more burdens on such persons or their families.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And the idea that section 7 of the MHCTA is being used for mental health management is entirely mistaken, as I have explained earlier and reiterate again.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would also urge Members to help clarify this mischaracterisation and put the minds of the mental health patients themselves and their families at ease, as Dr Wan Rizal has helpfully sought to do through his engagements with the community.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In reality, as pointed out so well by Dr Syed Harun, the vast majority of individuals with mental illness would not fulfil the threshold set out in this Bill for apprehension by the Police and, rightly so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, without being told or having been told previously, Police will have no idea who these patients are.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the circumstances that warrant Police's intervention, Police are well aware and minded to calibrate their responses, and let medical professionals take over as soon as practicable.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is the overriding priority of the Police if they are called to a scene and they make the assessment that most likely this person would be best served by having medical attention.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is the whole design of section 7 and the rules governing apprehension.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I have explained earlier too, this is not the same as arrest, where the person will be placed in a lock-up.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The amendments we are discussing are in fact to better achieve the objective of letting medical professionals manage persons with mental health issues, as my responses to specific queries will also show.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Ng and Mr Edward Chia asked about the Police’s procedures for responding to cases of attempted suicide.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such cases involve both persons who have, and persons who do not have mental health conditions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When attending to such cases, the key objective of the Police is to ensure the safety of the person and others around him.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If there is risk of imminent harm and a stand-off ensues, such as a distressed person standing on a ledge in a high-rise building, the Police’s Crisis Negotiation Unit, comprising Police officers and psychologists, will be activated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They will try to dissuade him from committing suicide.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After the Police have ensured the safety of the various parties, they may apprehend the person under the MHCTA if they assess that the person still poses a danger to himself, or others, and bring him to seek psychiatric treatment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If not, other relevant personnel may then be brought in to attend to the suicidal person and to provide the necessary support.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This may include mental health professionals from the IMH Crisis Response Team.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Ng and Mr Chia asked about treatment of individuals who have been apprehended.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These individuals will be assessed by the medical practitioners at IMH to determine the likely medical causes for their behaviour.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The medical practitioners may recommend further treatment in either inpatient or outpatient settings, or refer the individuals to social service providers to address their social needs where warranted, for example, where there is employment support and financial assistance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chia asked about collaboration between the Police and the Community Outreach Teams, also known as CREST teams, which are set up by AIC.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Where appropriate, the Police will refer persons with mental health conditions to the CREST teams in the region or to AIC, which will refer the cases to other appropriate mental health service providers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Keeping in mind that some of these individuals may well prefer to maintain their privacy and not have whatever action that they have taken be made known so widely so I think Police is also mindful of that and they will have to decide whether it is appropriate for them to make a referral.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Ms He's question on whether the Crisis Response Team may be expanded, Police and IMH are already reviewing this suggestion.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But in any case, even if the Police have some sense that this was so, for this idea to work, we will need to have sufficient numbers of such professionals on 24/7 standby, and for them to be able to respond immediately with the Police to all cases at all parts of our island.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Unfortunately, I think this will be very difficult to accomplish.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The practical approach is for the Police, after dealing with the danger, to refer such persons to mental health professionals for treatment or, as we discussed earlier, to other community support organisations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Choo, Ms He and Mr Ng asked how the Police assess whether the threat of physical harm is attributable to a mental disorder.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The role of the Police is not to assess or diagnose mental health conditions or disorders.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are not best placed to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police have access to reports of past incidents associated with the person, whether he had sought treatment at IMH then, and other relevant information including medical history from the family members, to aid their assessment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Police officers can also consult mental health professionals at IMH via a dedicated phone line.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police regularly update their training, conducted by suitably qualified professionals, to ensure that it remains relevant.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This point was reinforced by several Members, and we could not agree more the importance of training.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, Police officers undergo a mental health awareness course designed by the Agency for Integrated Care which helps the officers identify and respond to persons observed with indications of mental health conditions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Apart from training, officers are also guided by a specific set of internal SOPs, which are regularly updated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Mr Chua’s questions on amendment and implementation timelines, we will ensure that the amendments and the training provided to police officers will continue to enable them to intervene in a more timely manner while making decisions that underscore respect and empathy for persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Choo and Mr Yip alluded to the need for clarity on when the Police may make an apprehension.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms He also asked about the time frame police would now apply in the assessment for danger.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The powers of apprehension under the MHCTA have been in place since 2008.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The proposed amendments seek to allow the Police to intervene in a more timely manner, when the danger is there, even though it may not be immediately clear that the danger is imminent or when the person may turn violent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not practicable to be too prescriptive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Doing so could bind the Police officers’ hands or prevent them from acting quickly when they should.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Situations on the ground can be dynamic, and they need to be given the latitude to make quick decisions in difficult situations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The safety of the public and family members around such a person, and of the person himself, should be a priority.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Dr Syed Harun puts it, no meaningful medical treatment is possible without first ensuring the safety of the patient and rescuer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We agree with Mr Yip and Ms He that safeguards are nonetheless important.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Police ground response force officers don body-worn cameras which ensure accountability and transparency.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Their actions can be audited very easily because it is recorded.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the officers have breached the law and committed criminal offences, the Police will refer the matter to the Attorney-General's Chamber for criminal prosecution.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the officers are guilty of misconduct but it is not a criminal offence, the Police will conduct internal investigations and take disciplinary action as necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, it is not a case that you suddenly are going to go out and make apprehensions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, there is no anticipated increase in resourcing needs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police intervene only when the person poses a danger to himself or others around him.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police do not get involved in cases involving persons with mental health conditions but who do not pose any danger to himself or others.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Ng and Mr Choo asked about the requirement for the public to assist a Police officer when he is making an apprehension.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Criminal Procedure Code provides the same duty to assist a Police officer or any other person authorised to make an arrest.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The intent is for the Police to be able to reasonably call upon members of the public to assist them in preventing individuals with mental health conditions from causing further harm to themselves or others.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip asked how the amendment to the Police's obligations for non-arrestable offences apply to neighbour disputes or noise complaints, and whether such cases will be dismissed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Communal issues between neighbours are not and should not be matters for the Police to intervene.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do Members have any clarifications for Minister Teo?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: This relates to the High Court judgment in Mah.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When a person has been apprehended, the next course of action is to bring them to a medical facility for treatment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If there is a specific question on whether it conflicts with the specific part of the law that Ms He highlighted, with your permission, Sir, may I invite her to file a PQ so that we can deal with it properly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It probably does not impact the way in which the amendments ought to be considered.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I just wanted to seek clarification about the point made about the procedural difference as well between the apprehension and the arrest, which I think the Minister has clarified.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I said that probably at least three times, but I am happy to confirm again.
